A capacity factor is a measure of how often a power plant or renewable energy source is operating at its maximum capacity. It is calculated by dividing the actual output of the plant over a given period by its maximum potential output if it were operating at full capacity 100% of the time. For example, a wind farm with a capacity factor of 30% means that it produces electricity at its maximum capacity for 30% of the time, and at lower capacities for the remaining 70% of the time. This term is important in comparing the performance of different energy sources, including new nuclear and wind plus storage.

Dispatchability refers to the ability of a power source to generate electricity on demand, in response to changes in electricity demand or supply. In other words, a dispatchable power source can be turned on or off, or its output can be adjusted, to meet changing electricity needs. This is particularly important for wind power, which is an intermittent source of energy that can only generate electricity when the wind is blowing. Understanding dispatchability is crucial for evaluating the reliability and flexibility of new nuclear and wind plus storage systems.
